title: A hymn in Tilang
hook: Tilang holds Guru Nanak's hymn to Lalo about Babur's invasion, and its promise of a time for truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Tilang, where Guru Nanak's plea leans toward Persian. Your line: persian color. A new week starts.

When is the right time to say a hard, true thing? Right away, while it's raw? Later, when it's safe? Only to the people in charge? A page into the Tilang section, Guru Nanak gives his answer in the middle of a disaster. An army has come down from Kabul. Wedding songs have turned into songs of blood. And the hymn is addressed to one man by name, again and again: Lalo. Today: a hymn in Tilang, and what it does with the truth.
screen: `WHEN DO YOU SAY THE HARD THING?` → `AN ARMY FROM KABUL.` → `ADDRESSED TO LALO.`

segments.voice: Earlier on this path you heard this shabad as courage, and as a word told first to a working man. Today, watch its moves. First, it names what went missing. In paraphrase: modesty and dharma have both hidden themselves, and falsehood walks about as the leader. Before counting any damage, it says what vanished from public life: shame and right living. Second, who was pushed aside: the qazis and the brahmins, the religious officials of both communities, have lost their place. Third, who suffered, and it doesn't stop at one side. The Muslim women read their scripture and in their pain cry out to Khuda, God. Women of the Hindu castes, high and low, are counted in the same reckoning. Yesterday Tilang spoke in the words of Muslim neighbors; here, in the same raga, grief crosses the same line. Nobody's suffering is left out to make a point. Fourth, when. Near its close, on the next page, Guru Nanak says he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. That's the answer to the hook's question. Not when it's comfortable, and not only when someone powerful asks. When it's true, and the time has come. That's truth to power: the power never gets a vote on the timing. Whatever followed, the shabad was sung, kept and set in the Granth, where it is still sung in Tilang.
screen: `MODESTY AND DHARMA HAVE HIDDEN.` · `THE QAZIS AND BRAHMINS PUSHED ASIDE.` · `GRIEF ON EVERY SIDE IS COUNTED.` · `TRUTH AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `TRUTH TO POWER.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, listen to this hymn, often searched as jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee, or let one true thing come to mind that you haven't said yet; it might be small. Shape it into one plain sentence, without blame and without softening, and simply hold it, with no need to say it today, and with one Waheguru if you pray.
A hymn in Tilang. Guru Nanak's song to Lalo about the invasion: what vanished, who was pushed aside, who grieved, and truth told at the time of truth. Today's word.
Your line: truth to power. Truth at the time of truth, kind as well as true. That's day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn addressed to Bhai Lalo is sung in kirtan in Raga Tilang, and its line about speaking as the Master's word comes is quoted by some Sikhs as a standard for honest speech.

what a scholar hears: the hymn runs across ang 722–723; it counts both the qazis and brahmins displaced and the women of both communities suffering, and closes with Nanak speaking the word of truth at the time of truth.

notes: Paraphrase of the Tilang hymn at Ang 722–723 (saram dharam dui chhap khaloe, koor phirai pardhan; kajian bamana kee gal thakee; musalmaniaa parheh kateba kasat meh kareh khudai; jaat sanaatee hor hidvaaneeaa; sach kee baanee nanak aakhai sach sunaaisee sach kee belaa). Please confirm.

Kept to the text; no date for the invasion and no names beyond Kabul, Lalo and Khuda, which the hymn itself uses (Babur is named in the outline and in the hymn's later lines; not stated in voice to avoid a dated claim).
This hymn was taught at days 40 and 659 and cited at 1014; this day takes a new angle (the hymn's four moves and the grief that crosses communities) to avoid repetition.
